title: Understanding Decision Making
objectives: Distinguish normative, descriptive, and prescriptive questions about the same decision.
Explain how feasible alternatives, beliefs about consequences, and values support a rational-choice benchmark.
Explain why context-sensitive choice challenges a thin rational model as a stand-alone description without treating every contextual effect as irrational.
Map a visible choice onto the process through which it was already being made.

title: Structuring a Decision
objectives: Distinguish what is feasible from what receives serious consideration.
Develop new alternatives and distinguish fixed constraints from terms that can be changed.
Identify opportunity cost as the value of the best feasible alternative forgone, and distinguish it from an unrecoverable sunk cost.
Separate predictions about consequences from values over those consequences.
Assess information by whether plausible results could change action.
Explain how uncertain assumptions and the cost of further analysis affect a choice.

title: Limited Attention
objectives: Explain inattentional blindness and change blindness.
Distinguish top-down selection from bottom-up capture.
Redesign an information environment so that neglected evidence can enter judgment.

title: Predictive Mind
objectives: Explain perception as inference rather than recording.
Describe priors, sensory evidence, prediction error, and precision in plain language.
Explain how bodily regulation can anticipate the effects of an action, using thirst as an example.
Distinguish perceptual prediction from a decision forecast, and specify an observation that could distinguish two competing interpretations.

title: Expectations
objectives: Use controlled comparisons to distinguish changes in reported experience, behavior, and measured outcomes.
Distinguish an external prediction from a forecast that can alter physiology, behavior, treatment by others, or opportunity.
Record a forecast and design an independent test of how acting on it affects the outcome.

title: Valuation
objectives: Distinguish formal utility, psychological valuation, evolutionary fitness, and normative value.
Explain how body, identity, relationships, price, context, and developmental history alter subjective value.
Separate integral signals from incidental spillover without turning evolutionary origins into prescriptions.

title: Rationalization
objectives: Distinguish a reason, a justification, and a cause.
Explain how post-choice interpretation can alter memory, value, and later belief.
Use a dated decision record and rival explanations to make learning answerable to evidence.

title: Part 1 review
objectives: Transfer concepts across chapters to a new scenario.
Choose or evaluate a decision procedure, explanation, or calculation.

title: Intuition and Deliberation
objectives: Explain automatic and reflective processing without treating them as literal brain systems.
Diagnose a heuristic through its target question, cue, ecological fit, and feedback.
Distinguish monitoring a judgment from choosing how to check or revise it.
Decide when intuition deserves trust and when a structured check is warranted.

title: Availability, Affect, and Representativeness
objectives: Distinguish affect, availability, and representativeness by the question each shortcut answers.
Explain why vivid cases and coherent prototypes can hide denominators and base rates.
Redesign one risk judgment so that feeling, story, and statistical evidence remain visible but separate.

title: Confirmation Bias and Motivated Reasoning
objectives: Trace how an existing belief shapes search, interpretation, memory, and attribution.
Distinguish confirmation, motivated reasoning, self-serving attribution, and correspondence bias.
Separate biased evaluation of evidence from an expectation that changes the outcome itself.
Build a structured disconfirmation protocol with a prediction recorded before discussion.

title: Anchors, Halos, and Decoys
objectives: Explain anchoring and insufficient adjustment.
Separate a global halo or horn impression from dimension-specific evidence.
Test whether a preference survives removal or rearrangement of a decoy.
Explain how evaluating options together, separately, or through a different response task can change their apparent value.

title: Framing
objectives: Distinguish framing from priming, fluency, and choice architecture.
Explain how equivalent descriptions and different problem definitions alter judgment.
Build an ethical complementary-frame protocol.

title: Priming, Fluency, and Familiarity
objectives: Distinguish semantic and affective accessibility from familiarity and processing fluency.
Explain how environmental and emotional cues influence recall and, through it, judgment.
Explain how repetition can increase liking and perceived truth without adding evidence.
Redesign a message so that clarity improves comprehension without borrowing credibility from ease.

title: Base Rates and Bayesian Updating
objectives: Use complement, intersection, union, and conditional probability without changing the event or denominator.
Translate a Bayesian update into natural frequencies and select defensible reference classes.
Diagnose base-rate neglect, reversed conditionals, conjunction errors, and information dilution.

title: Randomness and Overconfidence
objectives: Explain why small samples, streaks, and clusters can look more informative than they are.
Diagnose regression to the mean and distinguish an apparent causal pattern, including superstition, from evidence that an action changes the outcome.
Distinguish three forms of overconfidence, use an outside view to challenge the planning fallacy, and score forecasts for calibration and resolution.

title: Part 2 review
objectives: Transfer concepts across chapters to a new scenario.
Choose or evaluate a decision procedure, explanation, or calculation.

title: Risk and Uncertainty
objectives: Compare expected value with expected utility in one consequential insurance decision.
Distinguish known risk, ambiguity, tail exposure, and the limits of risk-preference measures.
Produce an uncertainty-aware recommendation that separates process quality from realized outcome.

title: Prospect Theory
objectives: Use a reference point, value function, and probability weights to explain the fourfold pattern of risky choice.
Test whether a gain–loss effect reflects prospect theory or a competing mechanism such as ownership, attention, inertia, or switching cost.
Translate one choice across frames while preserving final states, probabilities, and meaningful exit.

title: Decisions From Experience
objectives: Distinguish a described distribution from the selective path a decision-maker actually experiences.
Diagnose sampling, stopping, recency, avoidance, and feedback mechanisms in one supplier-risk case.
Design a learning system that combines calibrated description with representative experience.

title: Mental Accounting
objectives: Diagnose how labels, brackets, payment coupling, and account-closing rules change economic choice.
Separate sunk-cost escalation from forward-looking value while preserving valid informational and implementation reasons to continue.
Redesign one budget or project account so it protects a goal without hiding substitution, total cost, or exit.

title: Intertemporal Decision Making
objectives: Use discounted utility and present bias to diagnose preference reversal without reducing it to weak willpower.
Separate time preference from liquidity, trust, uncertainty, utility curvature, and task representation.
Explain how connection to a future self can affect patience, distinguishing neural associations from intervention evidence.
Evaluate evidence on making delayed goals easier to pursue, including temptation bundling and voluntary commitment.

title: Habits, Wanting, and Self-Control
objectives: Explain how a repeated action can become a habit, and why frequency alone is insufficient to identify one.
Distinguish habits from habituation, and wanting an outcome from enjoying it.
Explain how reward predictions guide learning and pursuit, and why a near miss can encourage another attempt without improving its odds.
Use observations of cues, urges, and consequences to distinguish possible explanations of a recurring action.
Design a specific replacement response to a familiar cue and explain how repetition can make it more automatic.
Explain how suppression and self-blame can interfere with change, practice observing an urge, and respond to a lapse with a concrete adjustment.

title: Deciding for a Better Life
objectives: Distinguish the experiencing self from the remembering self, connect them to emotional well-being and life evaluation, and explain why their assessments can diverge.
Distinguish predicted, decision, experienced, and remembered utility, including the pleasure or distress of anticipation and recollection.
Recognize when one salient feature dominates a judgment of a whole life, and bring the omitted consequences into the comparison.
Distinguish social integration, perceived support, loneliness, and relationship quality while keeping association separate from causal evidence.
Build a decision audit that names the person, measure, horizon, relationships, distribution, rights, and freedom to revise.

title: Part 3 review
objectives: Transfer concepts across chapters to a new scenario.
Choose or evaluate a decision procedure, explanation, or calculation.

title: Strategic Interdependence
objectives: Explain strategic interdependence through three situations in which the outcome depends on other people's choices.
Distinguish personal preferences from expectations about others, including what they expect you to do.
Use equilibrium to describe choices that fit together, while recognizing why it may not predict actual play.
Explain how incentives, private information, and expectations about later intervention change strategic behavior.

title: Coordination and Focal Points
objectives: Construct and read a payoff matrix, then identify best responses and pure- and mixed-strategy equilibria.
Distinguish focality, payoff dominance, and risk dominance as explanations for which coordinated outcome people pursue.
Diagnose whether a coordination problem requires a focal point, common knowledge, credible assurance, or an agreed division of benefits and responsibilities.

title: Cooperation and Social Preferences
objectives: Distinguish a coordination problem from a conflict between individual incentives and collective gains.
Explain how continued interaction, reputation, and institutions can support cooperation, including the need for repair after mistakes.
Use differences between games to separate strategic incentives, social preferences, and expectations about appropriate behavior.
Explain how ingroup favoritism can restrict cooperation and how shared goals and a more inclusive identity can help rebuild it.

title: Social Norms and Conformity
objectives: Explain how informational and normative influence shape conformity, and distinguish changes in private belief from public compliance.
Separate information about what people do from what they approve, and explain how public behavior can conceal private beliefs or amplify an early judgment.
Redesign one meeting or norm message so private evidence is elicited before public influence begins.

title: Markets, Mispricing, and Bubbles
objectives: Interpret rapid responses to news and explain why a correct reading of a headline may arrive too late to earn an abnormal return.
Distinguish rapid information incorporation, no free lunch, and fundamental-value accuracy; evaluate historical return patterns against risk, costs, and competing explanations.
Explain how cash flows, growth, discounting, and financing affect asset values and how limits to arbitrage can allow mispricing to persist.
Explain negative and positive market feedback; compare historical bubbles and experiments on experience, liquidity, expectations, and trading rules without treating their evidence as interchangeable.
Produce a falsifiable market memo and a two-direction bubble dashboard with a robust action.

title: Social Influence
objectives: Distinguish changes in private judgment from conformity, compliance with a request, and obedience to an instruction.
Use experimental evidence to explain how favors, commitments, scarcity, and liking can influence a response.
Diagnose whether silence reflects withheld doubts, unshared evidence, mistaken beliefs about colleagues, or uncertainty about who should act.
Redesign one group decision or escalation process so evidence, ownership, dissent, and a safe path to correction are explicit.

title: Culture and Identity
objectives: Explain what experiments on visual context, cultural cues, and insult reveal about how situations acquire meaning.
Distinguish group-level tendencies from individual diagnosis and generate evidence that could correct a cultural interpretation.
Redesign one meeting or decision process so disagreement, dignity, and local verification can coexist.

title: Part 4 review
objectives: Transfer concepts across chapters to a new scenario.
Choose or evaluate a decision procedure, explanation, or calculation.

title: Persuasion
objectives: Distinguish belief and attitude change from agreement to a request and subsequent action.
Explain how credibility, involvement, argument quality, and autonomy affect responses to a message.
Use research to design and test a proposal that addresses the audience's actual concerns.

title: Storytelling
objectives: Distinguish a story from information, an example, and a vivid anecdote.
Explain how stories influence attention, simulation, identity, emotion, memory, and resistance.
Diagnose when a story adds decision-relevant meaning, when it adds distortion, and what evidence must accompany it.

title: Message Design
objectives: Explain what experiments on clarity and uncertainty reveal about credibility.
Use a drafting aid to organize a message without mistaking its structure for evidence.
Match the strength of each claim to appropriate evidence, comparison, and uncertainty.
Produce and audit a message that remains accurate, dignified, and genuinely rejectable.

title: Communication
objectives: Map how the same utterance can produce different interpretations.
Use grounding and perspective-getting to test a social inference.
Distinguish evidence about a claim from impressions of a speaker’s honesty.
Redesign a high-stakes message so its intent, context, action, and repair path are recoverable.

title: Connection
objectives: Explain how relationship quality and expectations shape the decision to connect.
Diagnose whether a difficult conversation calls for practical help, emotional recognition, or identity repair.
Use follow-up questions and checked paraphrases to make emotional concerns understood before moving toward a solution; build connection through appreciation and shared activities.
Produce a warm-honesty opening that separates observable behavior, experienced impact, inferred intent, and a testable request.
Complete a repair sequence that acknowledges harm, accepts responsibility, and specifies changed behavior.
Distinguish supportive ties from connections that bring different information and opportunities into reach.

title: Part 5 review
objectives: Transfer concepts across chapters to a new scenario.
Choose or evaluate a decision procedure, explanation, or calculation.

title: Negotiation as Joint Decision Making
objectives: Map a negotiation as parties, alternatives, positions, interests, issues, options, and implementation conditions.
Distinguish value claiming from value creation while managing information deliberately.
Explain how interests, group obligations, status, and decision authority shape a negotiation.
Produce a prepare–interact–implement plan for one joint decision.

title: Distributive Negotiation
objectives: Produce a preparation sheet containing BATNA, reservation value, target, estimated ZOPA, standards, and learning questions.
Make or answer a first offer using independent analysis and a defensible rationale.
Conduct and audit a concession sequence from opening through close.

title: Integrative Negotiation
objectives: Diagnose the interests and constraints hidden beneath a stated position.
Build a priority map that identifies differences capable of creating joint value.
Produce and evaluate a package trade that improves both parties without surrendering distributive discipline.

title: Designing Better Agreements
objectives: Produce a minimum viable agreement covering ownership, measurement, verification, review, failure, and exit.
Diagnose whether unclear priorities, forecast disagreement, sensitive claims, or process failure warrants an optional agreement-design module.
Add an advanced term only when its measurement, incentives, authority, and implementation burden are defensible.
Evaluate a contingent contract under different forecasts, risk exposures, and incentives, and distinguish mediation from arbitration.

title: Part 6 review
objectives: Transfer concepts across chapters to a new scenario.
Choose or evaluate a decision procedure, explanation, or calculation.

title: Behavior Design
objectives: Apply one five-step workflow: define the behavior, diagnose the bottleneck, redesign the decisive point, measure, and review.
Match a practical change to the obstacle it addresses.
Increase the feasibility of a desired action by reducing friction, and make an unwanted competing action harder to perform.
Anchor a new action to a reliable prompt and distinguish prompting, planning, and habit formation.
Compare immediate enjoyment, celebration, temptation bundling, commitment, skill building, and social support as ways to sustain action.
Distinguish follow-through from the outcome it is meant to improve, and plan how to resume after a lapse.

title: Choice Architecture
objectives: Diagnose where a menu, default, mapping, friction, timing, social signal, or feedback changes a choice path.
Compare nudges with boosts, incentives, mandates, and structural change for the same barrier.
Design and test an intervention that protects understanding, welfare, and meaningful exit.

title: Decision Hygiene
objectives: Build a proportionate judgment process before debating its answer.
Protect independent evidence, structured disagreement, and accountable use of models or AI.
Review forecasts, process, fairness, and outcomes without confusing luck with quality.

title: Deciding With Data and AI
objectives: Explain how growing data availability and falling costs of computation expand the practical uses of evidence.
Distinguish descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analysis, and recognize when a causal claim requires additional evidence.
Separate a prediction from a value judgment, an intervention effect, and an authorization to act.
Explain how AI, machine learning, and algorithms relate, and match tools to a specific decision task.
Explain why probability thresholds, data labels, and evaluation criteria embody human choices.
Design a small, testable decision workflow using data and, where useful, AI, with a baseline, an owner, and a learning rule.

title: Part 7 review
objectives: Transfer concepts across chapters to a new scenario.
Choose or evaluate a decision procedure, explanation, or calculation.
